title: Control Plane Governance: CTO/Head of Security Playbook for Private Deployments
content:
Purpose and audience:
This is a pragmatic playbook for CTOs, Heads of Security, and procurement leads evaluating Redwood Private (VPC / on-prem) for regulated workloads. The goal: give field teams short, confidence-building language, a technical template for security review, and concrete commercial/contractual asks buyers can use in RFPs or procurement decks.

Elevator pitch (one sentence):
Redwood Private provides a customer-controlled inference deployment with a minimal cloud control plane footprint — designed so you can enforce policy, retain custody of data, and audit every action without vendor-managed ingress to your sensitive networks.

Three core messages for executives:
- Data custody and auditability: The customer owns the runtime, keys, and logs; Redwood’s control surface is limited to non-sensitive orchestration endpoints and audited admin operations.
- Predictable economics and SLAs: Reserved capacity and optional out-of-band support contracts keep latency and uptime SLAs aligned with enterprise workloads.
- Built for regulated environments: HSM/KMS integrations, customizable RBAC and OPA-compatible policy hooks, and air-gap deployment options map directly to compliance requirements.

Common buyer objections and suggested rebuttals (short, conversational):
1) "We can't allow any vendor control plane access to our VPC."
   - Rebuttal: "We support a split-mode control plane: admin plane runs in your VPC and the provider control plane is limited to metadata-only endpoints. We can provide an audit record of every operator action and sign contracts to restrict vendor-initiated exec access to scheduled, auditable sessions with dual-auth."
2) "How do we prove you won't exfiltrate data?"
   - Rebuttal: "We can run in a private control plane with no egress for inference data, integrate with your KMS/HSM so keys never leave your boundary, and provide deterministic logs and attestation artifacts for every inference request. We also deliver an initial VM-level snapshot as part of the POC so you can validate runtime behavior offline."
3) "Upgrades and patching will break our certifications."
   - Rebuttal: "We offer a documented upgrade cadence with canary windows, staged rollouts, and the option for maintenance-only upgrades that run in isolated test slices first. We provide binary-level change logs and signing to support your change-control process."
4) "We need vendor indemnity and data residency guarantees."
   - Rebuttal: "We can include specific residency clauses, SCIM/SAML identity integration, and narrow indemnity language tied to our on-prem package; legal will work with you on SLA credit frameworks tied to measurable metrics."

Technical control plane patterns to present (textual diagrams and behaviors):
- Split Control Plane (recommended for highly regulated):
  * Admin / orchestration components deployed inside customer VPC or on-prem network (Helm charts / k8s operators under customer control).
  * Redwood control surface limited to a push-only artifact repository and signed operator bundles; no inbound API access to customer data plane.
  * Audit log shipping is one-way (customer-managed logging endpoint / SIEM ingest).
- Air-gapped On-Prem Mode:
  * Full control plane bundle delivered as an air-gap install kit; support via signed bundles and offline attestation tool.
  * Option for on-site professional services for initial install and upgrade windows.
- Minimal Cloud-Managed Control Plane (for lower-risk workloads):
  * Control plane runs in partner cloud region; customer data and keys remain in VPC with strict network policies + mandatory mTLS.

Security controls mapping (how to translate vendor features into buyer checklist items):
- Key management: "Must support external KMS/HSM (KMIP, CloudKMS) and customer-supplied keys (BYOK)"
- Access control: "RBAC + SSO integration via SAML/SCIM, support for SCIM provisioning and OIDC-based service accounts"
- Auditing: "Immutable, signed audit logs with export to customer SIEM and optional WORM storage"
- Network posture: "Default-deny, egress-filtered orchestration, optional private link/peering"
- Software assurance: "Signed binaries, SBOMs for each release, vulnerability scanning pipeline results"
- Attestation: "Signed attestation tokens for POC and production deployments (hardware root-of-trust where available)"

Suggested contractual language (plain drafts for legal teams):
- Data Residency: "Vendor shall not transfer, copy, or persist customer inference payloads outside the customer-defined geographic boundaries without prior written consent."
- Access Restrictions: "Vendor personnel access to the customer's environment will be restricted to scheduled sessions that are logged and require two-person authorization; remote access will be performed only under explicit change windows and with customer-specified bastion/telemetry in place."
- Audit Support: "Vendor will provide signed audit bundles and cooperate in third-party audits; vendor attests to producing a reproducible sequence of events for any requested timeframe within contractual limits."

POC checklist (what to deliver in the first 4 weeks):
Week 0: Pre-POC alignment
  - Provide one-pager architecture diagram tailored to customer's network.
  - Share SBOM and latest pen-test summary.
Week 1: Air-gapped / VPC install
  - Deliver deployment bundle and install runbook; customer completes install with vendor-observed session.
  - Validate KMS integration and that keys never leave customer boundary.
Week 2: Functional tests
  - Run latency and throughput benchmarks using customer workload; capture token-level cost estimates.
  - Exercise RBAC, canary rollout, and failover (regional fallback) scenarios.
Week 3: Security and compliance tests
  - Export signed audit logs into customer SIEM; run sample audit queries.
  - Deliver attestation artifact and SBOM verification report.
Week 4: Business review
  - Present runbook for upgrades, regression test results, and a proposal for production cutover + SLA terms.

Evaluation criteria template (scorecard to give buyers):
- Data custody (0-5): Are keys and logs fully under customer control?
- Attestation & auditability (0-5): Can customer reproduce runtime behaviour and provide artifacts?
- Upgrade safety (0-5): Does vendor provide staged, signed upgrades and rollback?
- Support model (0-5): On-call SLAs, local/onsite support options, and professional services availability.
- Cost predictability (0-5): Clear reserved capacity pricing and documented burst/overage rules.

Competitive notes (high-level):
- Versus public cloud-managed ML endpoints: Customers choose Redwood Private when they need policy-level control, attestation artifacts and guaranteed non-exfiltration; public clouds win on integrated managed services and procurement simplicity.
- Versus self-hosted open-source stacks: Self-hosting offers maximum control but requires significant ops lift. Redwood Private positions to remove that lift by delivering hardened installs, signed upgrades, and enterprise-grade support while preserving custody guarantees.
- Versus other inference vendors: Focus on measurable audit primitives (signed logs, SBOMs, attestations) and contractual access controls — most competitors emphasize performance SLAs but lack the same attestation/export artifacts.

Field scripts and set-phrases (short snippets sales can use live):
- "We will run the control plane components you care about inside your network; we only ask for push-only access to an artifact repo — no open inbound management APIs."
- "Before any vendor operator touches your environment we’ll produce a signed attestation and a video-recorded, customer-approved access session."
- "If you need a fully air-gapped install, we have an on-prem bundle and an onsite professional services option; upgrades are signed and staged so you control the change window."

Risk register (what legal/infosec will ask and where product must respond):
- Vendor access during emergency: policy + signed emergency access playbook, dual-auth requirement.
- Vulnerability disclosure: process and SLA for CVE remediation; offer temporary mitigations for high-severity issues.
- Third-party software risk: provide SBOM + mitigation commitments.

Next internal actions (ownerable items):
- Finalize an "attestation artifact" spec for product and engineering (owner: Riley Park, due: 2026-02-05).
- Prep an air-gap install kit FAQ and PS engagement playbook (owner: Samira Patel, due: 2026-01-30).
- Legal to draft sample residency and access clauses for sales toolkit (owner: Diego Alvarez, due: 2026-01-25).

Appendix: Evidence pack to hand to buyers (fast links and short descriptions):
- SBOM snapshot (last release) — binary list, hashes, vulnerability scan summary.
- Signed attestation template — example token + verification steps.
- Pen test executive summary — scope and remediation items.
- Sample upgrade runbook — step-by-step canary/rollback procedure.

Notes and open questions (for product + eng):
- Do we support hardware-backed attestation for all on-prem partners? If not, list recommended HW vendors.
- Can we automate SIEM export connectors for Splunk/Datadog? Priority: medium.
- What legal negotiation levers are acceptable for indemnity and residency? Need playbook from legal.

End of playbook — keep this lean, update as we learn more from initial enterprise deals.
